We are now a low-trust society, even compared to other wealthy societies around the world.You go to Scandinavia and these are much higher-trust societies. They handled Covid better. They handled the pandemic better because of that. America’s a very low-trust society. The balkanization of the media is a huge part of that. Even if you believe in one media institution, there’s another media institution that’s a competitor trying to tear that one down that’s going to tell you that they’re lying to you.The number of people I’ve talked to, and I also see this in focus groups all the time, where people will say, “I listen to Fox News and I watch Fox News and I also watch MS Now because I have to get both sides now.” People are now trying to seek out more partisan viewpoints or political viewpoints in order to make the judgments for themselves, which is a tough place to put individuals in. But because there’s so little trust in media in general, but also in the government and corporations, that’s what people are left to do.There was a report last year in Semafor that you had held talks with The Bulwark to discuss a partnership. Obviously The Bulwark started as a bunch of Never Trumpers. Is that enough expansion? You’re going to have a shared set of facts and probably some different policy prescriptions?The thing with The Bulwark is because they’re just so like-minded to us, we like doing a lot of stuff with them. Whether it makes sense as a business partnership you can put aside, because of the amount of cross-pollination between our shows. I’m always on Tim Miller’s podcast and he’s doing something with Lovett and Sarah Longwell’s doing something with Dan Pfeiffer.We think that by doing more stuff with them, their audience is exposed to us, our audience is exposed to them, and that just helps with our larger political mission. We see it more as a political alliance and partnership than it is a business partnership.The reason I’m asking this is I see the creator businesses getting bigger. You can see the creators raising money to do roll-ups. I think Johnny Harris is raising money to roll up more YouTube channels. Right next to that is the platforms that hate this idea. The platforms would prefer the army of teenagers working for free.Yes.The army of teenagers working for free never show up at YouTube’s door and say, “We would like better terms. We would like higher ad rates or we will withdraw our content.” It’s just, “We’re going to make more teenagers. You can leave.” We’ve seen this happen many times. Right now, something in the media ecosystem like Netflix is paying for podcasts and YouTube wants those people to stay.There’s something where the creator media has gravity. It has real audience, that audience is durable, and going from YouTube to Netflix might actually harm YouTube in some way. Whatever is happening there seems important. How do you think about Crooked in that dynamic? Would you ever go to YouTube and say, “We’re going to leave you for Netflix?”I have to say, once a bunch of podcasts were on Netflix and I started taking a spin through Netflix, I thought, “Even with the algorithm there, it’s really tricky to find those podcasts on Netflix.” Now, if you just have a really popular podcast and you have an audience, then that’s great.But I just think that, at least from my perspective, it’s just easier to find your content on YouTube than it is on Netflix. I don’t think the money would be more valuable than the audience growth that you’d get on YouTube.To bring this all back around, I’ve heard you say these midterms represent the end of the Trump era. Whatever this was, it was blissfully over. All the politicians are now influencers unto themselves. JD Vance is a creature of X, for better or worse. That is how that man communicates. Mamdani is a creature of TikTok. The House Oversight Committee made what can only be described as an NBA hype reel about lawyering up.Something has happened to our politics where this is how we communicate now. As you said, the Democrats are a big tent. They have a lot of differing priorities. We’ll see how that all gets expressed. What do you think happens now? Do you think they will be able to effectively communicate in the platform environment, in the media environment that we find ourselves in now?That’s going to be difficult over the next two years. You still need a president, you need a leader of the party, to be able to try to effectively communicate. The Democrats who were successful on Election Day, which are most of the ones who are running [in 2028], were successful because they were their own little creator economies in their campaigns and they weren’t trying to necessarily communicate to a national audience.A great example is James Talarico’s campaign. I got to know his speechwriter a little bit, and his campaign did something interesting there, which is they combined the speech writing and social media functions. They decided, “All right, this is a state rep in Texas who no one knows, and the way to become known is through storytelling. The oldest tactic in history.”[Laughs] Are you really doing the end of Game of Thrones in my show right now, Jon? Come on. Don’t do this to me. No one liked it.Right, no, me neither, me neither. Their social media presence was mostly TikTok, mostly Instagram, and it was just James Talarico telling stories really. It was giving speeches, but it was some of the oldest stories in human history, like David and Goliath. But I do think that [concerning] the whole “politicians as content creators” thing, there’s a way to do it where you are participating in the circus and then there’s a way to do it that is true to yourself and your values and the story you want to tell about where the country is and where you want to take it.If that story is compelling, then it will travel and break through even in this crowded media environment. The rise of vertical video allows for that kind of storytelling in a way that we haven’t seen in a while. After Barack Obama won the Iowa caucuses, we knew that every primary night he would get primetime coverage when he won and would be able to deliver a message to the whole country because everyone would be watching because it was primary night.We really focused on those speeches. For Talarico’s campaign, and for a lot of these other Democrats now, they have a million of those moments every day, but they still have to do the storytelling in order for it to break through. The most successful candidates figured out how to do that storytelling in a really compelling way that wasn’t just “I’m going to tell a joke on Twitter” or “I’m going to do the hype reel” if I’m the House Oversight Committee.That is an effective way of getting people’s attention, but not necessarily holding their attention. If you are a politician today, you’ve got to figure out a way to get people’s attention, but then to hold it. And to hold it, you have to have a compelling story to tell.My favorite piece of election day media was Rob Sand, the governor-elect of Iowa doing the Fleetwood Mac video where he drank the cranberry juice and longboard. I thought, this is great. I don’t know what the purpose of this video is, but I’m having a good time. And maybe that’s all you needed on this day was to just channel some vibes.Then you got to actually go make some policy proposals. You have to fill potholes in New York City and then sit there and make videos about the filled potholes, which the Mamdani administration is particularly good at doing. Do you think this class of Democrats has that ability, even though they have a president who’s threatening to veto everything that they’re going to do?I do think they have the ability. They’re going to be able to communicate. They’re going to be able to have hearings when they’re holding big tech CEOs and administration officials accountable. Those will be moments. They’re going to also have moments where they get to exert power over the government funding process.I personally think we’ll be headed towards several shutdowns because that’s going to be the main mechanism for Democrats to get their way. But also for the next two years, Donald Trump and the Congress are just not going to be the main focus. The main storyline of the next two years is going to be the presidential primaries.I remember Democrats had a huge win in 2006, and then people can barely remember until the financial crisis what George Bush and the Democratic Congress were up to between 2006 and 2008, because everyone was focused on the Republican primary for president and the Democratic primary for president, because they were two wide open primaries. Once we get into 2027, you’re going to have a million primary debates on both sides.Donald Trump’s obviously going to try to insert himself into the debate by trying to play kingmaker on the Republican side so that he can continue to get attention. And God forbid there are external events and crises that we have to deal with, then everyone’s going to be paying attention to Trump and the Congress. But the machinations of what’s happening inside the Congress I think will be the secondary story of the next two years.You mentioned tech regulation. Actually, that’s where I want to end. I’ve often described hearings in Congress with tech CEOs as content capture sessions. That’s what we’re doing. Instead of Apple having the new iPhone and all the creators rushing in to take photos of it, here’s Mark Zuckerberg and all the senators are going to rush to yell at him and we all make our videos and that’s the end of that. Nothing ever seems to happen.Our audience is particularly nihilistic about it. You can yell at these CEOs all you want, but they just get their own way. There’s a lot of opportunity for oversight, particularly around AI, particularly Jensen Huang, the opportunity to do oversight over Nvidia and the Commerce Department and the FBI, whatever is happening. Boy, is there a lot of opportunity to oversight there.How do you think that looks? We cover this often from a technology lens on the show. You cover it from a political lens on Offline. What do you think this looks like?I know what I want it to look like. Because of where we are with AI development, I am more interested in oversight that actually changes the situation, that finally puts some guardrails or restrictions on the development of super intelligence, AGI, recursive self-improvement, whatever you want to call it, than just show trials where we all get to dunk on Mark Zuckerberg.My biggest concern is we don’t have time to wait for a Democratic president or even a Republican president who’s actually going to do something to regulate the development of AI because by the time we get to 2028, it feels like the horse will have well left the barn. It’s already left the barn. I’m curious, over the next two years, can Democrats and Republicans in Congress actually force some kind of regulation or at least coordination among the AI giants to stop us from going off the cliff here?If I had to point to a realignment, it’s what I mentioned at the top. Surveillance feels like a glimmer of a realignment, and then data centers and AI feel like the glimmers of a realignment. You shouldn’t just take the economy away from people. Regardless of partisan lean, I think for most people, to your point about agency, feel you can’t just do that. You have to show up and make the case.That is enough for a wholesale realignment. Those two issues are enough for these parties to totally scramble. And you’re going to get pro-business Democrats saying, “We’re going to have to do something to work with these guys.” You’re already seeing it. There’s James Talarico saying, “I wish Elon would just stay in his lane and stay out of politics, but we need him as a great businessman.”You’re seeing it on the Republican side: “We got this wrong. We need to regulate the Big Tech companies. I’m anti-data center too.” In this environment where they basically have a little less than a year to make headway before the primary cycles begin, what do you think the steps are?I worry that when I listen to a lot of these Democratic politicians and Republican politicians, all of them, there’s only a handful that seem to really understand the technology. You talk about regulation with people and they say, “Yeah, we need safeguards.” Safeguards could be anything from its effect on children and chatbots to making sure that we don’t lose human control of artificial intelligence.I feel like the cybersecurity stuff and the bio stuff — and then where recursive self-improvement goes — are the big areas where I would want to see Democrats and Republicans get together. Even if they can’t pass laws because Trump doesn’t want to do anything to hurt the AI companies because he looks at it and says, “The stock market’s tied to this, the economy’s tied to this, and I don’t want to do anything to hurt the economy and got to beat China and all that bullshit” — which is not bullshit — but you can’t answer every single concern about runaway artificial intelligence and losing control with the word “China.” Trump seems to be doing that and some other politicians as well.But he can’t anymore because there are Chinese spies.[Laughs] Right. He’ll try. He’s going to try.This is going to change the terms of this debate. An empowered set of China hawks are saying, “Look at the spies.”But even if there were no spies, they also lifted the export controls before to send the chips to China.Because of the sexy spies. It’s right there.But it was also probably in their financial interest, even if there were no sexy spies. I do think that even if you can’t get regulations passed, there needs to be even the convening power of the federal government with these companies to sit them all in a room and say, “We have to work on this together.”And international diplomacy with the Chinese. We’re not going to get out of this in one piece by Trump and Xi meeting and saying, “Yeah, it was a great meeting and we both think AI is important and we’re going to keep talking about it.” You have to actually get down into the details and the weeds here over the next two years or else I think things could get really bad really fast.I can hear our audience screaming in their cars. I can predict their YouTube comments. The YouTube AI should just start doing predicted comments.No, I’m worried it’s not going to happen. I’m with it.They’re screaming nihilism at you. They’re saying, “None of this will happen.”I worry about the same thing. I think public pressure around this is the only avenue here right now, as long as Trump’s in power. People inside the companies, people outside the companies continue to talk about this to raise the alarm, to sound the alarm on this and to tell people about the dangers. I don’t think that’s necessarily going to get us to the best place, but it’s the best chance that we have right now.My hottest election take has been that this election proved that X is irrelevant, that Elon Musk’s purchase of X is now a failure on every dimension. It’s shrunken users. He’s definitely not making as much money as even failed Jack Dorsey Twitter used to make.Again, criticism of Elon’s X is in no way praise of the Jack Dorsey Twitter. That was a poorly run company that allowed this outcome to happen, but it’s not making more money. It doesn’t have more users. And now we can see the absolute limit of its political influence.Yeah. It has outsized influence on the political debate because of all of the journalists and politicians who are on it. What we saw in the last cycle is the limits of the political debate to influence the decision of the electorate.I would connect that to the people at these companies needing to keep raising the alarm because the place where they keep raising the alarm is on X and they’re not great communicators when it comes to the public. They can’t make the case for data centers.In fact, mostly what the public hears is, “We might kill all of you.” Another anonymous researcher has surfaced to say that they’re quitting their job instead of killing you all. Now what? Do you think that there’s a better way to make that jump to make that case?Yes, because every time I see one of these posts — I just saw someone who said, “I just came from San Francisco and I’m so scared. This is crazy,” and I said, “All right” — but then there’s never a good explanation for most people as to why. What is the scary part?San Francisco is just Milwaukee with rich people. I need to make this as clear as I can. It is not as scary as people want it to be.But I do think that there is — speaking of storytelling — a storytelling function missing here where it’s great that people are speaking out and saying this is dangerous, but then you want to say, “Okay, how is it dangerous? Give us the steps from recursive self-improvement to the robots killing us all, or robots don’t have to kill us all, but [they can create] a horrible cyber attack or biological weapons.”I do think painting the picture of actually how this could affect people and continuing to sound the alarm on that and then saying, “If we did these things, we might be able to slow this down or stop it” is important too. Because if you’re just going to scare people without providing a path to how to fix the problem or how to rein it in, then eventually, it’s just going to be noise. “Oh, another person’s screaming about how we’re all going to die. What am I going to do about that?”There’s some very basic political science in here. Why we have a government is to counterbalance industry. Again, are we telling stories on social media? Abdul El-Sayed is doing political science 101 — “I’m a capitalist.”Adam Smith is like “monopoly is a danger to capitalism,” and this is eighth grade. He’s just doing eighth grade at people all the time to explain that the role of government is to constrain industry in some way or provide some sort of framework for industry to make lives better for people instead of just collecting profits. That is the role of government.AI is the ultimate collective action problem or prisoner’s dilemma, whatever you want to call it. It is why we have governments, not just a government in our country, but why we have the United Nations and an international order of countries that even if they don’t agree, even if they are adversaries, can sit down and figure things out together because there are just some problems that none of us can solve on our own.There are some set of Republicans who say, “We should go back to being free markets. We should go back to this thing.” Do you think that they are going to have any influence in this next turn?No.Fair enough.They might have influence. A lot of them have finally realized that they have lost the public on this. I was interested to hear the All In pod after the election, and Chamath Palihapitiya especially, talking about, “We thought that maybe everyone would trust that if the asset managers and the rich people did well, they would ultimately do well. That’s clearly not the case.” It’s like, “Yeah, obviously.” But I think a lot of them just didn’t realize that.That was the longest winded, most VC coded version of the voodoo economic speech I ever heard.It was. It is wild. I’m like, “You’re just getting that now? Oh, cool. Great.”“We’re just saying trickle down didn’t work again, but in this way.” Okay, that’s fine. That ecosystem is closed.It is.I’m thinking of Andrew Sullivan warning the Republican Party of epistemic closure in 2000 on his blog on The Atlantic. And now we’ve landed at a closed podcast ecosystem where I’m pretty confident everyone’s buying views for each other, just to be clear, to make it look bigger and more influential than it is. But the fever has to break there too. The CEOs can’t all just be creators. They have to run their companies and make their shareholders money and operate in a new political environment. How does that fever break?Silicon Valley has always been incredibly insular like this. Even back in the social media age, even when we dealt with them in government. I got to know some of these folks afterwards when I moved out here. They view everyone who works in government as, “Politics is just an engineering problem to solve. The fact that it’s this messy means you must be a bunch of dummies running the place.”This is the theory behind DOGE. “If we can just go in there and bring our technology and bring our brilliance, we should solve all these political problems.” But political problems are problems of the human condition. It’s people trying to figure out how to live together and divvy up scarce resources and figure out how to govern themselves.That’s really messy and you actually need some social and political expertise to do that. You can’t just be a genius coder or a capitalist and feel like this is going to solve everything. But I think for a long, long time in Silicon Valley, they’ve seen the government as just another problem to be solved by engineering or capital allocation. And it’s just not. It’s never going to be that. Politics is going to be much messier.I think it’s all of that. And then one I would add to it is they also see it as a rich source of revenue, which is why you have seen so many of them move into being defense contractors. It’s an inarguable way to get a bunch of money from the government, to say, “We will build you weapons and AI systems for blah, blah, blah.” All of them have done it regardless of their professed values. The idea that YouTube is run by a defense contractor is mind-blowing to me.I know.But it is just straightforwardly true, right?Yeah.You can see the idea that SpaceX is a defense contractor and we might turn down Starlink in Ukraine and Trump has to go on television and be like, “I have no idea what happened.”Right, and Elon’s just sitting there saying, “I can flip a switch whenever I want.”Yeah, there’s something there. Again, to come back to collective action problems and the role of government to actually control these companies and control the industry. It seems like it’s up for grabs in a way that suggests you and I should probably talk again very soon.It feels like in these next two years, that realignment, the glimmers of it that I see are either going to come true or not. I’ve been wrong before, but something about the relationship between government and the tech industry is bound to change.I agree.Jon, this has been great. What’s next for Crooked? Tell people what to look out for.We just finished Crooked Con, which was wildly successful. We had over 3,000 people to talk about the results of the election, and now we’re just trying to figure out how to cover this primary.You’re already in primary coverage?The primary has begun. Even though people have not announced their candidacies yet, by the time we get to winter, it’s going to be in full swing.So DeSantis, Rubio and JD.Ted Cruz.Oh, God.I know, and then a million people on the Democratic side.You’re already covering it. All right. I was hopeful that we would get some sincere legislative action, but we’re doing primaries.We’ll do both. It’s going to happen at the same time.I love it. Well, thank you so much for being undercover. This has been amazing.Thanks for having me.Questions or comments? Hit us up at decoder@theverge.com. We really do read every email!Decoder with Nilay PatelA podcast from The Verge about big ideas and other problems.SUBSCRIBE NOW!Follow topics and authors from this story to see more like this in your personalized homepage feed and to receive email updates.Nilay Patel

content_html_zh:
Today, I’m talking with Jon Favreau, a political commentator and cofounder of Crooked Media. You probably know Jon best from a little show called Pod Save America, which Jon started with a group of fellow Obama staffers in the wake of Donald Trump’s election in 2016. It’s now one of the most popular podcasts in the country.

Since then, Pod Save America and the company created around it, Crooked, have become one of the major success stories of independent liberal media. So one of my central questions for Jon was why he thought Democrats swept the midterms earlier this month and, more importantly, why it happened now — especially after a wave of tech billionaires made big swings to the right while buying huge pillars of the information ecosystem.

That’s Elon Musk buying Twitter and turning it into X, Mark Zuckerberg sucking up to Trump while tearing down Meta’s content moderation infrastructure, the Ellison family buying stakes in TikTok, turning over the leadership of CBS News and now potentially CNN while integrating Warner into Skydance… the list goes on. How did they all miss the huge swing in the mood of the public — or, more apocalyptically, fail in their attempts to control the media and thus influence the public?

Crooked itself is also just a fascinating business, as all creator businesses are. When we think of what you might call news creators, we tend to look to the right — after all, conservative media have been building an alternative, direct-to-consumer pipeline since the dawn of talk radio.

But Jon and his fellow Crooked cofounders created a reliable template for liberal creators, and it’s working. Crooked hired its first CEO a few years ago, now offers more than a dozen original shows, and has a staff of around 100 people working on everything from live events to political advocacy. Jon tells me the subscription business has crossed 65,000 members.

So of course I wanted to know how Jon feels about topics we cover a lot here on Decoder: online distribution, the platform power of YouTube, and how you balance running a media business that has to make money with a newsroom that, ultimately, has a political mission and a strong point of view.

I’m excited to have you here. I’ve been on Offline with you. It was a really fun conversation.

I have a million ideas about what to talk about with you. I want to talk about Crooked as a creator company in this particular moment in media. I feel like we have to start with the midterms though. The blue tsunami is here. It feels like a repudiation of the billionaires owning all the social platforms, the billionaires owning all the broadcast networks.

I think it’s a repudiation of a government that came into power with the chief promise of bringing inflation down and making life more affordable, and it didn’t do that. If you’ve looked at the last couple of elections, people voted a party into power and they said, “Everything’s too expensive and I want stuff to be cheaper and I don’t want to be struggling. Can you do something about it?”

And then either they try to do something about it or they fail to do something about it or like Trump, you don’t even try at all. You actually make life harder, and then people say, “The propaganda that’s coming out of Fox or any of these right-wing platforms doesn’t matter. I fill up my car and gas is expensive and I don’t know if I’m ever going to be able to afford a house because interest rates are up, et cetera, et cetera.”

You can say whatever you want to say, but people’s lived experiences end up being more salient than the messages that they get from politics.

Is it just that simple?

I hate that it’s that simple.

It’s just, “Gas prices are up, just throw the bums out.” But I would say the last 10 years of politics are, “Can I tweak policy into reality?” We’ve seen it happen several times. “Can I wage memetic warfare on the American public until these Republican talking points are the framework in which all further conversation must happen?”

We’ve seen it happen on the left too. I think Defund the Police is a great example of a thing that just spiraled out of control and maybe turned an election. But in particular, we’re going to wake up and the Fox News machine is going to define the terms of the debate, and then we’re going to wake up and whatever’s happening on Twitter is going to define the terms of the debate. That has been how it’s worked for an awfully long time, and “the gas prices are too high” and “this war is stupid” maybe just defeated it.

It works to a point, but there are certain conditions that messaging and media just can’t overcome, especially for the party in power or forever, whoever’s running the White House.

The same was true with Joe Biden. Joe Biden could go out there and say, “We passed this bill. We gave money out. We gave the checks out and things are getting better and we’re just recovering from Covid. You haven’t felt it yet, but it’s getting better and look at the economic statistics.” And people just said, “No, I don’t feel that yet. So I’m going to maybe give Donald Trump another try, even though I think he’s a shitty guy and I don’t like him very much.” But maybe they remember the economy of the first term being good.

We dealt with this when Obama ran and became president in 2009. They thought, “Financial crisis. Can’t stand Bush anymore. I’m going to try Obama.” And then Obama gets into office and for the first two years, the financial crisis is over, but the recession is still there. People are still out of work.

So they said, “I know you passed healthcare and I know you passed the recovery act, but I still can’t find a job. The economy just still doesn’t feel great to me.
